articles.title: I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense
articles.author: Adam Annaccone, Clinical Associate Professor of Kinesiology, University of Texas at Arlington
paras: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

That moment stayed with me. I’ve spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I’m a clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children’s athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages.

And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it’s easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I’m more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them.

As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I’ll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what’s appropriate as their children’s sports experiences intensify.

When I’m watching my children play, I’d rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I’m happy to help. They usually decide when we’re done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That’s fine too.
Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.

Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to make decisions about their participation.

As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn’t mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.

I’ve heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn’t always easy when your child is part of a team.

But more training doesn’t automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. Training places demands on the body, and athletes need time to adapt.

The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with increased overuse injury risk and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.

As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they’re experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn’t keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.

Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop coordination and a range of movement skills. The International Olympic Committee recommends varied physical activity and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize.

Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to want to continue participating, research shows. When young soccer players were asked what made sports fun, they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won’t accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.
Leaving the game at the field

In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn’t and what needs attention. But children don’t need a performance review every time they climb into the car.

I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I’ll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that’s fine too.

Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and sports came up relatively infrequently. They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don’t establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.

No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I’m comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I’m far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.

articles.title: What the measles vaccine’s ‘97% effective’ rating means for Pittsburgh parents
articles.author: Rebecca Smullin Dawson, Associate Professor of Biology, Allegheny College
paras: Pennsylvania is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, with more than 1,400 confirmed cases and six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, according to statistics compiled by the state.

Each new case brings a new warning of a measles exposure in that community. Exposures have occurred at hospitals and doctors’ offices, grocery stores and restaurants, and K-12 schools and universities.

Exposure alerts come with the same instructions: Check your MMR vaccine status, and watch for symptoms for the next three weeks. People are told that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. The underlying message is that if you’re vaccinated, you’re protected.
The MMR vaccine is highly effective at preventing disease, but it isn’t a guarantee. People may hear that 97% figure and wonder about the other 3%.

Parents ask me: Should I be worried? How do I know if my kid has measles? Do I need an MMR booster? Most recently, my teenage daughter texted me to ask about her MMR vaccine status. She was worried about what would happen if she were exposed.

These are questions I can answer as both a mother and an epidemiologist in northwestern Pennsylvania. I became both at once. My daughter was born at the start of my doctoral program, and I read epidemiology textbooks aloud to her while studying for my comprehensive exams. I defended my dissertation on my son’s due date. I’m a better mother because I’m an epidemiologist, and a better epidemiologist because I’m a mom.
Are these measles exposure alerts cause for alarm?
The advice in each public measles exposure alert matches the guidance doctors follow when a patient may have been exposed.

Everyone is asked to watch for symptoms, whether or not they’re vaccinated. The number of unvaccinated people across Pennsylvania is growing. As a result, many communities, including Allegheny County, no longer have herd immunity.
Four of the over 1,400 confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania were people who had been vaccinated. These cases are known as breakthrough infections.

The term “herd immunity” wasn’t coined until 1918. That year, a veterinarian wrote about an outbreak of “contagious abortion” in sheep and cattle, a literal herd. Today, herd immunity means that the risk of disease for susceptible people, those without immunity, drops when they are surrounded by people who are immune.

In other words, if the people around you are immune, you’re unlikely to get sick even if you’re susceptible. For measles, that protection depends on about 95% of people being immune. In a school or community where fewer than 95% of people are vaccinated, measles can spread more easily.
In Allegheny County, 93.8% of children are fully vaccinated against measles. Some neighborhoods are above 97% uptake, while others are below the necessary 95% needed for herd immunity.
What happens after an exposure?

Measles exposures are announced publicly by the Department of Health and local healthcare providers. During a measles outbreak, public health departments may get in touch with close contacts to alert them to an exposure.

Public exposure alerts, like the one made in October after there was a measles exposure at a Target near Pittsburgh, are also used. Public alerts are for settings where exposed people can’t be identified and contacted individually. Measles is so contagious that a single case can infect up to 18 susceptible people.
Measles spreads through the air and through respiratory droplets, like those released when someone sneezes. The virus can also survive outside the body, lingering in the air and on surfaces.

Imagine I have measles and walk into my local grocery store. I’m contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after. Every time I breathe out, I release virus particles into the air, and those particles can stay infectious for up to two hours. If I sneeze in the produce section, the virus can survive on surfaces for up to two hours.

However, if you’ve had measles or were vaccinated with two doses of the MMR vaccine, you are protected. Two doses provides 97% lifetime protection against measles. This means that even without herd immunity, fewer than 3% of individuals with immunity are likely to contract measles. Adults who have had measles, or who have documentation of the recommended doses of the MMR vaccine, don’t need a booster.

People who were vaccinated between 1963 and 1967, or who aren’t sure which vaccine they received, should talk to their primary care provider about whether they need another dose. This is because the measles vaccine used between those years was not as effective as the MMR vaccine that is currently given.

Today, children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old. Because the vaccine is given in early childhood, people born in the early to mid-1960s are the most likely to have received the older vaccine. People born before 1957 are generally considered immune, because measles was so widespread then that almost everyone caught it as a child.
What are the symptoms of measles?

Symptoms of measles include a high fever that can reach 105 degrees Fahrenheit (40.6 degrees Celsius), a cough, a runny nose and conjunctivitis, also known as pin keye. These symptoms overlap with those of other respiratory viruses, such as flu and COVID-19.

Most people with measles develop a red, blotchy rash. It starts on the face and spreads down the body, like paint poured from a bucket. People who are immunocompromised or were previously vaccinated, even with one dose of the MMR vaccine, may not develop the rash. Between 25% and 40% of immunocompromised people with measles never get the rash.
A telltale sign of measles is Koplik spots, tiny white spots inside the mouth that can show up a day or two before the rash.
Why does measles keep making headlines?

Measles can have serious consequences. About 1 in 20 people with measles develop pneumonia, and up to 3 in 1,000 cases end in death. Children younger than 5 and adults older than 20 are most likely to experience these severe complications.

Without herd immunity in many communities, measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths in Pennsylvania are likely to keep rising. The state Department of Health reports community spread of measles in 14 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties.

Each of these cases is mostly preventable with the MMR vaccine. The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning it was no longer spreading continuously here. This year’s outbreak shows how quickly that can change and the negative health consequences it can have in our communities.

articles.title: Is natural toothpaste really as good as fluoride? Tooth decay expert on the difference
articles.author: Aylin Baysan, Professor of Cariology in relation to Minimally Invasive Dentistry, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Natural, herbal and organic toothpastes are becoming familiar sights on shop shelves, often promoted as healthier alternatives to conventional products. Some contain ingredients such as aloe vera, neem or green tea. But before changing toothpaste, there is one important question to consider: does it contain fluoride?

Fluoride is a mineral that helps protect teeth against decay. Some toothpastes marketed as natural contain it, while others do not. The words on the front of the tube cannot tell us whether a product will protect our teeth.

These terms are often used interchangeably, although they mean different things. “Natural” usually describes ingredients derived from natural sources. “Herbal” refers to plant-based ingredients, while “organic” generally describes ingredients produced to particular farming standards. None of these labels, on its own, shows that a toothpaste can prevent tooth decay.

The range of products is considerable. A 2021 UK study examined 500 toothpastes, from 95 brands with alternative formats such as tooth powders and solid toothpaste tablets. Nearly a third contained no fluoride, and some did not clearly state their fluoride content. The study examined products available to buy, so it cannot tell us how many people actually use fluoride-free toothpaste.
Why fluoride makes a difference

Tooth decay begins when bacteria in dental plaque, a sticky film that builds up on teeth, feed on sugars from food and drinks. They produce acids that damage enamel, the hard outer surface of the tooth. Over time, this can lead to holes, or cavities.

Fluoride helps enamel resist acid and repair early damage before a cavity forms. Its benefits are supported by decades of research. A 2019 Cochrane review, which brought together results from 96 studies, found that brushing with fluoride toothpaste reduced tooth decay compared with brushing with toothpaste without fluoride. Reviews bring together findings from multiple studies to assess the overall evidence.
Yet people sometimes switch to fluoride-free products because they believe natural ingredients must be safer or healthier.

In a 2019 letter to the British Dental Journal, my colleague and I described a dental student who had developed several cavities after changing to a fluoride-free organic toothpaste. The student had other risk factors, including a history of sugary snacking and infrequent dental visits. We can not say that this single case cannot show that the organic toothpaste caused multiple decays, but this clearly illustrates why checking for fluoride is important, even for people who brush their teeth regularly.
The evidence for herbal toothpaste

Some toothpastes and mouthwashes contain plant extracts, including green tea, aloe vera and neem, a tree traditionally used for oral hygiene in South Asia. These ingredients may help control bacteria and gum inflammation – also called gingivitis – which can cause redness, swelling and bleeding when brushing.

A 2024 review of earlier research suggested that some herbal oral-care products, particularly mouthwashes, could reduce plaque and gum inflammation as effectively as conventional products. But many of the studies were short, and their methods with the results varied. This makes it difficult to know how well particular ingredients work over time.

Reducing plaque and gum inflammation is useful, but it does not prove that a toothpaste prevents cavities. There is insufficient evidence that herbal ingredients can replace fluoride’s established protection against tooth decay. A toothpaste can contain plant ingredients and fluoride, so consumers do not necessarily have to choose between them.

Charcoal toothpaste is another product often marketed as natural, particularly for whitening teeth. A 2023 review found limited evidence that charcoal toothpastes whitened teeth better than other options. Most studies also suggested that they could be more abrasive: they might wear away the tooth surface through rubbing. However, most of the research was conducted in laboratories, so it cannot establish how much wear occurs with everyday use.
How to choose a toothpaste

The simplest way to choose a toothpaste is to check the fluoride concentration on its packaging. In the UK, NHS advice is that adults should use toothpaste containing at least 1,350 parts per million (ppm) fluoride. This means at least 1,350 parts of fluoride for every million parts of toothpaste.

Children need the right strength and amount for their age. The NHS recommends at least 1,000ppm for children under three, using just a smear. Children aged three to six should use a pea-sized amount of toothpaste containing 1,000–1,500ppm fluoride. From age seven, the recommended concentration is 1,350–1,500ppm.

Tooth-brushing twice a day for about two minutes, including last thing at night, and spit out the excess toothpaste rather than rinsing immediately with water would be beneficial. This leaves fluoride on the teeth for longer. A dentist can advise if someone needs extra protection against tooth decay.

Lastly, natural ingredients may have a useful place in oral care, and better long-term studies could establish more about their benefits. But labels such as “natural” or “organic” are no substitute for evidence. Whatever else a toothpaste contains, an appropriate amount of fluoride currently remains one of the simplest and cost-effective ways to protect teeth.

articles.title: This weightlifting technique can help older adults stay fit and independent as they age
articles.author: Liam T. Pearson-Noseworthy, Distinguished Teaching Fellow, School of Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation, Northumbria University, Newcastle
paras: If you’re over 60 and have started lifting weights, you’ve probably been told to take it slowly. Lift steadily, lower steadily, keep it controlled.

This may sound like sensible advice, but lifting slowly isn’t always better. While the technique may have an edge when it comes to building strength and muscle, lifting with speed may be the better option if you want to stay fit and keep moving well for years to come.

Most people associate weightlifting with building muscle and strength. But lifting can also build power (how quickly our muscles can produce force). This aspect of fitness fades earlier and faster than strength does as we age.

Part of the reason for this sits inside the muscle itself. Our muscles are made up of two types of fibres: slow-twitch fibres, which are built for endurance, and fast-twitch fibres, which are built for speed and help produce force quickly. While our slow-twitch fibres tend to hold up fairly well with age, our fast-twitch fibres tend to shrink and weaken.

The weakening of these fast-twitch fibres can have a significant impact on daily life as we get older. Even things as simple as climbing stairs or crossing the road before the lights change all benefit from power.

Muscle power may even matter more than strength when it comes to staying mobile. A study of 839 older adults in Italy compared how much power people could produce pushing with one leg with how hard they could push against a fixed resistance. The researchers found those with low leg power were two to three times more likely to have limited mobility than those with low strength.

Power matters for trips and falls too. When you catch your toe, your standing leg has to push off quickly and forcefully, which gives your other foot time to swing forward and land in the right place. Being less able to generate muscle force as you age may mean it’s harder to stop yourself from falling if you trip.

A study of 94 older adults compared people who’d had a fall in the past year with those who hadn’t. Both groups had similar strength in their knees, but those who’d fallen had less leg power, estimated from how quickly they could stand up from a chair five times.
Because the study looked back at falls, it can’t tell us whether low power caused the fall or if recovering from the fall caused the loss of power. But it fits with the trip research.

The good news is that training can help. In a very small pilot study of just nine people, 16 weeks of leg strength training increased how hard they could push off with their legs. Those who trained also tended to respond better after a trip than those who didn’t, though the difference was too small to be certain.
But in order to build muscle power, you need to lift a little differently than you would to build strength.
Training strength usually means lifting and lowering the weight at a controlled, comfortable pace. To train power, you still lower the weight under control, but try to lift it quickly and with force.

A large review of 20 trials and 566 older adults compared lifting fast with lifting more slowly. Lifting fast gave a bigger boost to muscle power and also provided modest benefits to everyday physical function.
When it comes to strength, the picture is more mixed. In that same review, strength and muscle gains were the same either way.
My 2022 review of 12 trials conducted in people over 60 found strength gains leaned towards faster lifting – though this finding wasn’t very robust, as the studies were small and often low quality.

I also conducted a trial in 31 untrained adults aged 60 to 79 where they did one leg press session a week for six weeks. Whether they pushed fast or slow, their strength, everyday function and quality of life all improved. However, the slow groups tended to gain a little more strength, while the fast groups tended to improve more on everyday tasks.

A 2026 review of 16 studies in adults aged 60 and over found that slower lifting tended to come out ahead for muscle size and strength, while faster lifting tended to come out ahead on tests of everyday physical function.
So technique may matter depending on your goals. Slower lifting may build somewhat more strength and muscle, while faster lifting may help more with everyday tasks.

But it’s important to note that fast lifting isn’t a cure-all. That same review of 20 trials found this technique made no clear difference when it came to improving balance. For preventing falls and improving balance, the strongest evidence is for balance and functional exercise – movements that copy daily life, such as stepping and turning. Combining these exercises with strength training may cut the number of falls by about a third.
Building power doesn’t mean you have to change your entire weightlifting routine. All it takes is one small simple technique change.

When lifting, lower the weight slowly and under control. Then, push it back up as fast as you can while keeping good form. Pick a light-to-moderate weight, something you could lift perhaps 15 times with good form, then stop well short of that, at around eight reps, so every rep still moves quickly.

The same is true if you’re performing bodyweight exercises at home. If you’re doing a chair squat, for example, aim to sit slowly before standing up as quickly as you safely can. Use your hands on the armrests if you need to.
The weight itself doesn’t have to move fast. What matters is that you’re trying to move it as quickly as you safely can.
Weightlifting has many benefits for our health as we age. Just make sure to train power as well as strength to help you stay mobile for longer.

articles.title: Delayed international support has hampered efforts to contain and treat Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo
articles.author: Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi, Assistant Professor of Healthcare Administration, Fayetteville State University
paras: I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next.

I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services.

That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids.

Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading.

More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference.

The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths.
This is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo.
The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC remain serious concerns.

The DRC has extensive experience with responding to outbreaks, and African institutions are coordinating a continental response. Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably.
Ebola follows human movement. In October, Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also reported an imported case around the same time.
Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later.
These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders.
What international support looks like now

International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance. The U.K. announced a contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million).

In October, the World Bank described $426.6 million in current and planned financing for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly $3 billion in international pledges following a September mobilization effort.
But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak.

In 2014, Britain helped expand treatment and safe-burial operations in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners.

That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further.
According to the WHO, massive cuts to international aid over the past year diminished a quicker response.

The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care.
Building connections with everyday people

My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect.

That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola. Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools.

The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions.
Reaching affected communities
In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for expanded laboratory and treatment capacity and faster delivery of supplies.

But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement due to ongoing conflict, in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households.

The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety.

There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved. This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak.

Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The Tumaini vaccine trial, begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine.
The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss.
I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them.
Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi was the past West Africa Regional Program Lead for Africa CDC.

articles.title: Mammograms can do more than detect breast cancer – they also offer important clues on heart health
articles.author: Matthew Nudy, Assistant Professor of Medicine and Public Health Sciences, Penn State
paras: If you’re a woman over 40, you have no doubt heard your doctor tell you to get a mammogram as part of routine screening for breast cancer. But there’s another reason, too.

A mammogram can show no sign of breast cancer and still reveal something worth discussing with a doctor: calcium deposits in the medium-sized arteries that carry blood to the breast. These calcium deposits may offer a clue to a woman’s future heart health.

I’m a cardiologist who studies cardiovascular health around menopause. My colleagues and I have investigated how mammograms might help identify women who are at increased risk of heart disease and stroke. Artificial intelligence now makes these calcium deposits – called breast arterial calcification, or BAC – easier to measure.

In October 2026, Maryland became the first U.S. state to require mammography centers to notify patients in writing if these calcium deposits are found in their mammograms. Other states may institute similar rules soon. Research shows that these calcium deposits are a robust marker for cardiovascular risk, and I expect its adoption to grow.
Here’s what women need to know about calcium deposits in the breast – and what they should do if their mammogram shows they have them.
What is breast arterial calcification?

Breast arterial calcification is calcium buildup in the walls of medium-sized arteries that carry blood through the breast. On a mammogram image, the calcium deposits appear as parallel white lines tracing those vessels.

This finding is not a sign of breast cancer. And it differs from the fatty and calcified plaque that can narrow arteries supplying the heart muscle. In the case of breast arterial calcification, the calcium lies mainly in the artery’s muscular wall, where it is associated with blood vessel stiffening.

Finding breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not, by itself, establish that a woman has heart disease or a blocked heart artery. But research has now clearly shown that this marker signals that a person’s risk of these outcomes is elevated.
It’s important to remember, however, that its absence does not rule out cardiovascular disease or an increased risk of heart attack or stroke.

Doctors have known about breast arterial calcification for decades, with studies in the 1980s linking it to diabetes and advanced kidney disease. Early findings about its relationship with heart disease were mixed, and many studies were small and relied on radiologists’ visual review of mammograms.

In 2022, my colleagues and I published the results of a 10-year study in which radiologists reviewed mammograms of more than 1,000 women to identify these calcium deposits. Women who had them had about three times the odds of developing coronary heart disease and five times the odds of having a stroke compared with women who didn’t, even after taking age into account.

To confirm that breast arterial calcification in mammograms predicts cardiovascular risk, we assessed 45 published studies involving more than 68,000 women, in a type of study called a meta-analysis. This work, published in 2026, found that women who had these calcium deposits in their breast arteries on a mammogram had roughly twice the risk of stroke, heart failure and death from any cause, and nearly three times the risk of dying from heart disease, compared with women who did not.

The studies we analyzed differed considerably in design and quality, so these averages cannot precisely predict an individual woman’s cardiovascular risk. Also, while these findings establish an association between breast arterial calcification and cardiovascular disease, they do not show that calcium in the breast arteries causes those health outcomes.

Radiologists can see breast artery calcium on a routine mammogram. But there’s no common standard for grading and reporting how much calcification is present. AI tools which are being used more commonly by doctors can measure how much is there using the same images, with no extra radiation.

These calcium deposits become more common with age, so my colleagues and I used AI to assess data from more than 100,000 women in nine countries in order to map how calcium builds up in breast arteries by age. We developed and tested a metric that, when added to standard tools, improved doctors’ ability to accurately predict a woman’s risk of cardiovascular disease.
Integrating as a new risk marker

Maryland became the first state to require a notice about breast arterial calcification in screening results. The goal is to give women who have it a reason to talk with their doctor about heart health.

The bill’s sponsor modeled the law on a 2023 regulation on breast density notices, which required mammography centers to inform patients and their doctors about their breast density and its link to cancer detection. The breast density rule was first implemented in Connecticut and then adopted by many other states, before becoming a nationwide requirement.

An Australian trial called TIM-TAM will test whether using breast arterial calcification to guide care improves measures of heart health. Researchers still need to find out whether treating women based on the presence of breast arterial calcification prevents heart attacks or strokes. But research already shows that the marker has a link to cardiovascular disease, and I expect it to follow a similar pattern of adoption as reporting breast density.

Until other states adjust their requirements, look for “breast arterial calcification” or “vascular calcifications” in the radiologist’s report. Mammography centers’ reporting practices vary, so some reports may omit BAC even when it’s visible. Some imaging centers offer an optional AI review for breast arterial calcification as an out-of-pocket add-on to a screening mammogram.
What this means for your care

On its own, the presence of breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not determine whether someone needs a heart test or a new prescription. But in my view, this marker can provide a useful nudge to get an updated assessment of cardiovascular health.
Your doctor may suggest a blood pressure measurement and blood tests for cholesterol and kidney function. An estimate called eGFR describes how well the kidneys filter blood.

Your doctor can use these results alongside age, smoking, diabetes and other information in the American Heart Association’s PREVENT calculator. It estimates the chance of developing cardiovascular disease over the next 10 years for adults ages 30 to 79 who are not already diagnosed with cardiovascular disease.

You can then discuss with your doctor which steps could make the biggest difference for your heart health depending on your risk. That might mean finding ways to move more, choosing foods that are good for your heart or getting help to quit smoking if you smoke. Depending on your overall risk, your doctor may also suggest taking a statin to lower your cholesterol or starting or adjusting blood pressure medicine. These treatments can help lower your chances of a heart attack or stroke.
A routine breast screening visit can thus become an opportunity to help women understand their cardiovascular risk and take steps to lower it.

articles.title: An ADHD diagnosis can be a map to guide a person through challenging territory – not to avoid it altogether
articles.author: Deldhy Nicolás Moya Sánchez, Psychiatrist and Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM)
paras: Picture a young person who walks out of my office with a new ADHD diagnosis and feels relief. There is finally a name for years of missed deadlines and unfinished paperwork.
A few weeks later, they use that name to end an argument at home about an unmade bed and a pile of unopened mail, saying, “I can’t do that, I have ADHD.”

In another scenario, a student asks me for a medical note excusing them from a written assignment. Not extra time, not a quieter room, not help breaking the work into steps: They want the assignment dropped.

I often see both situations in my Mexico City clinic. They raise the same question: Does a diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder explain why a task is harder? Usually, yes. Does it settle which tasks the person should stop attempting? Rarely.

I am a liaison psychiatrist at the National Medical Center “20 de Noviembre” in Mexico City and a professor of medicine at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. My work deals with how psychiatric diagnoses land in a person’s daily life, including how anxiety and ADHD can mask each other. I sign several of those school and work notes every week.
Researchers have started to measure something I see constantly in the clinic: how much room a diagnosis takes up in how a person sees themselves.

Used as a map, a diagnosis shows where the difficult ground is and the best route through it. For instance, mornings may be when a patient falls apart, so we plan for them: medication, more structure and a few skills to practice. Used as an alibi – an excuse to avoid blame – a diagnosis marks the whole territory as off-limits.
Research suggests these two uses lead to very different lives: one in which someone gets through the day and another that shrinks around the diagnosis.
When the label takes up all the room
Psychologists who study chronic illness use the term “illness identity” for how far a diagnosis gets folded into a person’s sense of self.

A Belgian study of adolescents and young adults who have Type 1 diabetes described four ways a person can relate to a diagnosis: rejection, which is acting as though the diagnosis is not there; acceptance, which is “this is part of me, but only part”; enrichment, which is “it taught me something”; and engulfment, which is when it overshadows everything else.

Engulfment is high when someone can no longer describe who they are, what they want or what they are good at without the diagnosis taking precedence. The condition stops being something they have and becomes how they define themselves.

In 2025, an Israeli team surveyed 154 adolescents with ADHD about how much their diagnosis had shaped their sense of self. The researchers found that how engulfed participants felt predicted their quality of life more strongly than how severe their symptoms were. Of the four patterns, engulfment was the only one that explained why more severe symptoms coincided with a worse life.

The same research group found a similar pattern in a second study. In 66 adolescents, the more the diagnosis had taken over, the worse participants did on executive functioning, self-management and quality of life measures – in plain terms: planning ahead, starting a task and running their own routines.

These are snapshots, not experiments. They show that self-identity and well-being are linked, but they cannot tell us which one is driving the other. Even so, the pattern matches what parents describe to me as the moment their child stops saying “This is hard for me” and starts saying “This is what I am.”
‘It’s my brain’ can dampen effort
The brain differences in people with ADHD are real. Yet the way clinicians, teachers and parents explain a diagnosis can feed a disempowering loop.

Meta-analyses pool the results of many studies. One, co-authored by University of Melbourne psychologists, found that when a mental health problem is explained in biological terms – as a matter of genes or brain chemistry – blame goes down, which is good.
But a second meta-analysis, by another group of psychologists from Melbourne, found that brain-based explanations raise pessimism about recovery, which is not good.
The same explanation that lifts the blame can also lower the expectation of change.
Avoiding something usually makes it more threatening

One type of support can keep someone engaged with a task they find hard: an essay broken into steps with a deadline for each one, or a teacher who checks in at the start of a lesson rather than at the end. Another kind can take the task away.
The first builds skill. The second teaches that the task really is impossible.

Researchers who study childhood anxiety call that second kind “family accommodation,” and they mean something specific: A household gradually reorganizes itself so the child never has to face what frightens them. Someone answers the phone for the teenager who dreads phone calls, or the family stops having people over because visitors make the child anxious.

In schools, “accommodation” means something else: a change to the setting, such as extra time or a quieter room, so the student can still do the task. To avoid confusion, I call this school version “support.”

Nobody is asking families to be harsher or less understanding. But a Spanish meta-analysis found that the pattern of removing the feared situation is linked to more severe anxiety in children and adolescents.

A randomized trial showed that treating only the parents worked as well as treating the child. Parents were taught to respond supportively while stepping back from rescuing their child from what frightened them.

Teachers and school staff can also steer students away from hard tasks, often without realizing it. When a panel of experts reviewed school supports given to 76 anxious students in treatment, some pushed the student toward the difficult task and others pushed them away from it. Students with social anxiety most often got the ones that let them skip exactly what they feared: being seen and heard by their classmates.
Support and treatment are not the same thing

Educational supports are by far the most common response to ADHD in schools. Many families ask me for a letter requesting extra time on exams. One study found improved reading comprehension for college students with ADHD – but about as much improvement for their peers without the disorder. So extra time helps, but not the way a treatment does.

Most supports show no benefit specific to students with the disorder. That does not make them useless; several help any student. It means they are not treatment: A student can have numerous supports for years while the attention problem stays where it was.

After a diagnosis, the practical work focuses on medication, therapy, structure and a list of tasks that are broken down into smaller parts. I hand every patient that list, written down, before they leave.
Where this leaves the person in my office

When I write a school or work note, three things belong in it. First, the specific task the person struggles with. Second, the support that keeps them engaged with that task rather than away from it. Third, a date to review it: a support nobody looks at again stops being a clinical decision and becomes a permanent feature of someone’s life.
A good diagnosis does not remove responsibility. It moves it. The question stops being: “Why can’t I?” Rather, it becomes: “What do I work on, and with what help?”
The young person who learned to say “I can’t, I have ADHD” is not wrong about the diagnosis. They just have the rest of the sentence left to write.

articles.title: Commotio cordis: how a blow to the chest can stop the heart
articles.author: Adam Taylor, Professor of Anatomy, Lancaster University
paras: A recent incident during a Spanish Segunda División match between CD Tenerife and FC Andorra resulted in the tragic death of Tenerife player Jesús de Miguel. Although no official statement has confirmed the cause of his death, some reports suggest it could have been commotio cordis. This is a rare but well-known medical condition that can cause sudden cardiac arrest after a blow to the chest.

Commotio cordis means “agitation of the heart”. It was first described by doctors in the 1850s. In 1932, researchers in Germany identified three factors that help explain how it happens: the type of impact, its speed and where it strikes the chest. A sudden, sharp blow is particularly dangerous.
The heart sits inside the chest, protected by the ribs and the sternum, the flat bone at the front of the chest. Its lower tip points towards the left side of the body.

Unlike other muscles, the heart contains specialised muscle cells that generate their own electrical signals, allowing it to beat without conscious effort. It contracts thousands of times a day to keep blood circulating around the body, adjusting its activity to meet changing demands.

Heart muscle also does not tire in the same way as the muscles we use to walk, run or lift things. It can keep working throughout our lives because it relaxes between beats, giving itself time to recover.

This relaxation depends on a carefully timed electrical process. During part of each heartbeat, the heart’s cells reset their electrical charge so they are ready to contract again. This stage is known as the T-wave and can be seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG), which records the heart’s electrical activity.

During this brief period, the cells are normally less likely to respond to another electrical signal. But a powerful blow to the chest can send energy through the body’s tissues and disturb the electrical activity of the heart.

For commotio cordis to occur, the impact must happen at a very specific moment in the heartbeat. The vulnerable part of the T-wave lasts for roughly 30 milliseconds – just three hundredths of a second. A blow during this tiny window can interfere with the heart’s normal electrical rhythm.

The result can be ventricular fibrillation, one of the most serious heart rhythm disorders. Instead of contracting in a coordinated way to pump blood around the body, the heart’s lower chambers, called the ventricles, begin to quiver chaotically.
Blood can no longer circulate effectively to vital organs, including the brain. This causes cardiac arrest, in which the heart stops pumping blood properly and the person loses consciousness.

One unusual feature of commotio cordis is that the heart and surrounding tissues can appear completely normal afterwards. There may be no structural damage to the heart muscle, coronary arteries, ribs or sternum. This distinguishes it from cardiac arrest caused by injuries that physically damage the heart or chest.

The condition is rare but life-threatening. It is most commonly reported in children and teenagers aged four to 18. Most recorded cases involve males, who account for 94% of sporting cases and 93% of non-sporting cases.

Younger people may be more vulnerable because their chest bones and muscles are still developing. Their chest may offer less protection against the force of an impact reaching the heart. Women account for a larger proportion of non-sporting cases, at around 13%.

Football has seen deaths linked to commotio cordis before. A study examining sudden deaths in football worldwide between 2014 and 2018 recorded 617 player deaths. Among players aged 35 and younger who died suddenly while playing, 9% had, or were thought likely to have had, commotio cordis. In 11 cases, the impact came from a football hitting the chest. In three, it came from an opponent’s fist or elbow.

The condition has been reported more frequently in other contact sports. Baseball is often cited as the sport with the highest number of cases. Ice hockey, American football and lacrosse have also recorded more deaths than football.

One of the best-known recent cases involved NFL player Damar Hamlin, who suffered commotio cordis during a televised match. Medical staff responded immediately and saved his life. He returned to playing nine months after his cardiac arrest.

The speed of treatment is crucial to survival. Research suggests that when emergency treatment begins within three minutes, survival is more than 70%. If treatment takes three to five minutes, the chances fall to around 50%. After five minutes, they drop to approximately 25%.

Outside sport, commotio cordis can happen during assaults or road traffic collisions. Survival in these situations depends partly on whether someone nearby recognises what has happened, starts emergency treatment and has access to equipment such as a defibrillator.

Researchers believe commotio cordis deaths are probably underreported. This may be because it can be difficult to distinguish the condition from other causes of cardiac arrest, particularly when nobody witnesses the original impact.

Greater awareness of commotio cordis beyond cardiology, alongside the development of a national registry, is helping researchers understand the condition better. These efforts, combined with faster emergency treatment and improved access to defibrillators, could increase the chances of survival for people who experience it.

articles.title: HIV prevention medication is highly effective, but it can complicate blood donor screening
articles.author: Jaid Debrah, PhD Candidate, Blood Safety & Virology (PrEP/GBMSM), University of Oxford
paras: Taking medicine to prevent HIV might seem a good reason to feel confident about being able or eligible to give blood. Yet people taking pre-exposure prophylaxis, known as Prep, cannot donate while using it, and must wait for three months after their last dose before doing so.
Prep is taken by people without HIV to reduce their chance of acquiring the virus. According to the NHS, daily Prep is around 99% effective when taken correctly.

But if someone acquires HIV while taking Prep, the medicine can make the infection harder to detect. If an infected donation passed through testing undetected, it could transmit HIV to someone receiving the blood. Donation rules provide an additional safeguard against that possibility.

Research I carried out with colleagues found drugs used in Prep in some blood donations in England. These medicines have other uses, so their presence cannot confirm why someone took them. Our findings also cannot establish whether donors understood the restrictions, and we did not demonstrate HIV transmission through donated blood.
Our findings raise a question for blood services: how can they explain the restrictions clearly while supporting people’s use of effective HIV prevention?
Why Prep can make HIV harder to detect

If someone acquires HIV while taking Prep, the medicine can limit the virus’s ability to multiply, reducing the amount in their blood. It can also delay or weaken the production of antibodies, proteins the immune system makes in response to infection.

Blood services test donations for signs of HIV. These include genetic material from the virus and antibodies produced by the body. Research examining blood samples from studies of Prep shows that these medicines can make an infection harder to detect. Someone may have HIV before the tests can reliably identify it.
This helps explain why blood services ask questions about a person’s health and medication as well as testing their blood. Those answers provide information that a test result alone cannot supply.

Under UK blood donation guidelines, people must wait three months after their last Prep tablet before donating. For Prep given by injection, the waiting period is two years after the last injection. People must also meet the other conditions for donating blood.
Long-acting injectable Prep can remain in the body for months after injections stop. The waiting periods apply regardless of sexuality, even when someone would otherwise be able to donate.
How donation rules have changed
Blood donation rules have become more inclusive. In 2021, the UK introduced individual assessments following a review known as Fair (For the Assessment of Individualised Risk).

Previously, men who had sex with men faced restrictions that applied to them as a group. Under the revised approach, donors are asked the same questions about recent sexual behaviour, regardless of gender. This allows more gay and bisexual men to donate while maintaining safeguards for people receiving blood.

For example, anyone who has had anal sex with a new partner or multiple partners must wait three months after the last such contact before donating. Recent Prep use remains a separate reason why someone must wait.

Someone taking Prep might understandably feel reassured by its effectiveness and assume that tests on donated blood provide an additional safeguard. Explaining how the medicine can affect those tests should therefore be part of explaining the donation rules.

We tested blood samples collected in 2023 from 84 male donors in England. Their blood showed evidence of current or past syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection. Six samples, or 7.1%, contained both medicines used in a common type of Prep tablet.
The same medicines can also be used to prevent HIV after a possible exposure, or as part of treatment for someone who already has HIV. Finding them does not establish that a donor has HIV.

Our wider analysis found that donations showing evidence of current or past syphilis increased from about four to ten per 100,000 donations between 2018 and 2024. This does not establish that Prep or changes to donation rules caused the increase.

Because we tested a particular group of donors, these findings cannot tell us how common Prep use is among everyone who gives blood. Nor can they tell us whether people knowingly disregarded donation rules or misunderstood them.
Making the guidance easier to understand

The reason for the waiting period should be explained wherever people receive information about Prep and wherever they check whether they can donate blood. Knowing how a medicine can affect test results may make the restriction easier to understand.
Blood services should also make it straightforward for people to ask questions privately. Donors need to feel able to discuss medication and sexual health without expecting to be judged.

The different waiting periods for Prep tablets and injections make clear guidance especially important. Someone familiar with the three-month wait after taking tablets could otherwise assume that the same rule applies to injections.

People should not stop Prep simply to become eligible to donate blood. Anyone considering a change should discuss it with their doctor or nurse at a sexual health clinic, as stopping removes its protection against HIV.

Prep remains a major advance in HIV prevention. Explaining why people taking it need to wait before donating can help protect those receiving blood while supporting people’s use of medicine that protects their own health.

articles.title: Why one positive E. coli sample put a Pittsburgh-area community under a boil-water advisory
articles.author: Sarah Fakhreddine, Assistant Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: A boil-water advisory was issued on Nov. 2, 2026, by officials in Center Township in Beaver County, 25 miles from Pittsburgh, after a routine sample tested positive for coliform bacteria, including E. coli, according to the township’s water authority.

The advisory stayed in place while the authority kept testing, and Central Valley School District students stayed out of school buildings and attended class remotely on Nov. 3-4 as a precaution. The authority lifted the advisory on Nov. 4.
A single positive sample of E. coli can upend daily routines for an entire community, from what people drink to how they wash dishes, and leave residents wondering how worried they should be.
Two environmental engineers, Sarah Fakhreddine and Marlee Shaffer, explain why E. coli in tap water is a red flag, how boiling kills harmful germs, and how utilities decide the water is safe again.
How does E. coli get into drinking water?

When E. coli is detected in a drinking-water system, it means the water may contain harmful bacteria, viruses or parasites. Most strains of E. coli don’t make people sick, but E. coli is a common bacterium that lives in the digestive systems of people and animals. That’s why scientists use it as an indicator: Its presence flags that water has been contaminated by human or animal waste, which can carry germs that do cause illness.

A drinking-water system treats water so it is safe for people to drink and delivers that clean water to customers’ taps. Water can become contaminated during treatment or delivery, as it moves through the system’s pipes.

If there’s a problem with the treatment process, harmful pathogens may not be fully removed from the water. Or treatment may be working well, but a pipe breaks somewhere in the system and pressure drops. That can allow contaminated water to enter the pipes that deliver water to homes and businesses.
Why can one positive sample trigger a boil-water advisory?

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency sets a goal of zero E. coli in drinking water. A single water sample is a snapshot of water quality at the time and place it was collected. Because drinking water systems are interconnected, with water flowing through them, a problem in one location might mean water elsewhere could also be contaminated.

How much of the system is affected depends on where and why the problem occurred. It can take time for a utility to find the problem, fix it and test more water samples. A boil-water advisory helps keep the public safe while the utility investigates and addresses the problem.
What does boiling the water do?

Boiling water kills harmful bacteria and protozoa and inactivates viruses that might be in the water. High temperatures damage key structural parts of these microorganisms, leaving them unable to multiply and cause infections.

Research shows that at the temperatures water reaches when it boils, most harmful microbes are killed in under a minute. It can also help to keep some bottled water on hand in case you are unable to boil water.
How do water utilities determine when the water is safe?

Water utilities must show the water is safe and get approval before lifting a boil-water advisory. They have to investigate what caused the E. coli contamination, fix the problem and then keep testing to make sure no more samples come back positive. They share this information with their state or federal regulatory agency, which decides whether the utility has met the requirements to lift the advisory.
In Pennsylvania, the state Department of Environmental Protection requires a utility to show two consecutive days of negative samples after addressing the problem.
Why can’t kids go to school during a boil-water advisory?

In a school cafeteria, for example, an advisory affects not just drinking water but also the water used to wash fruits and vegetables, cook food and wash dishes. Meeting those requirements can be challenging, depending on the school’s size, its resources and whether it can get other sources of water, such as bottled water that has been transported in by truck.

Some schools may be able to stay open and comply with the advisory, while others may decide to close or switch to virtual learning to ensure safety. Children can be more vulnerable than healthy adults to waterborne illnesses, so compliance by schools is especially important.

articles.title: Stair climbers are said to boost fitness, strength and bone health — here’s what the evidence actually says
articles.author: Dan Gordon, Professor of Exercise Physiology, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: The stair climber has seen a huge surge in popularity on social media in recent years. Proponents of the exercise machine rave about its benefits – claiming it can boost cardiovascular fitness, strength and bone health.

Evidence shows the stair climber does have many benefits when it comes to health and fitness. While it doesn’t always win out over other types of cardio, there are a few key areas where it has an edge.
One reason for the stair climber’s popularity is that it’s thought to provide a high-intensity way of boosting cardiovascular fitness.

But when researchers compared the cardiovascular effects of exercising at the same relative intensity on a treadmill versus a stair climber, they found that those using the stair climbers had lower heart rates and oxygen consumption scores. This meant that stair climbing put less stress on the cardiovascular system, which may ultimately lead to smaller fitness gains.

That said, stair climbing has still been shown to be just as effective as brisk treadmill walking in lowering blood pressure. A comparison of stair climbing versus treadmill running also showed it improved cardiorespiratory fitness and even promoted similar increases in running performance.
So the stair climber is about comparable to running when it comes to improving cardiovascular health.
Another reason the stair climber is preferred by many gym goers is because it’s said to improve muscle health and strength more than other forms of cardio.
Indeed, stair climbing has been shown to engage more lower body muscles than walking or running.

Stair climbing also engages these muscles for longer and with more forceful contractions than walking. The more a muscle is activated and the longer it is held in one position, the more tension it develops. The greater the tension, the larger the physiological adaptation.

Perhaps unsurprisingly is that stair climbing has been shown to cause changes in muscle size that are similar to those seen in people who did conventional strength training using a leg press. These gains in muscle size were also associated with improvements in strength.
However, as this study was only conducted in older adults, it’s not clear if these results would also apply to younger people.
The changes in muscle size that are seen in stair climbers are greater than those seen in people who do treadmill walking or cycling.

An additional benefit of the stair climber may come from using the machine backwards. Walking downstairs activates more muscles than walking upstairs does. This is because our muscles have the additional job of braking so we don’t fall or lose balance. This will improve stability while walking.
The stair climber is sometimes recommended because it’s said to place less force and stress on the joints and bones.

When you run on a treadmill, the impact force (when your foot hits the ground) is equivalent to around two to three times a person’s body weight. For stair climbing, the impact force is a little lower – around 1.6 times body weight.

Stress, on the other hand, reflects the amount of force that goes through a joint during an exercise. So although stair climbing appears to place less impact force on the joints, a comparison study found the stair climber placed eight times greater stress on the knee than running outdoors on level ground did.

This makes sense, as to climb each step the foot needs to be in contact with the stair for a longer period than it would be in contact with the floor while running. So if you want to avoid putting your joints under too much stress, the stair climber may not be for you.

However, stress and impact forces aren’t always a bad thing. Evidence increasingly shows that stress to joints and bones may be crucial in maintaining bone health and reducing the effects of osteopenia and osteoporosis. And, despite its lower impact forces, stair climbing has been shown to help control osteoporosis and osteopeania.
The stair climber is therefore a great exercise even if you have joint issues or experience some pain. Just remember to start off slowly, doing small amounts of exercise at a time.

Another reason the stair climber is popular is because it is claimed that the machine will help you burn more calories – and therefore lose more weight. But the evidence backing up this claim isn’t quite so favourable.

A small study of 30 men compared how many calories participants burned when working out at maximum effort on the treadmill versus on the stair climber. The study found that the stair climber group burned around two calories fewer per minute than they did on the treadmill.

The reason for this difference probably lies in the total amount of muscles being recruited during each exercise. When running on a treadmill, the whole body is engaged – including our upper body muscles. But during stair climbing, the upper body muscles are used far less. Many people even use the handrails for safety, so there’s little arm swinging for momentum.

So for people whose primary goal is weight loss or weight management, the treadmill may be the more effective option as you burn slightly more calories. Though long-term weight loss success will ultimately depend on maintaining a consistent exercise routine.

Despite the hype, the stair climber isn’t that much more beneficial than other types of cardio when it comes to our health and fitness. But it does appear win out over other forms of cardio when it comes to strength and muscle.
If you’re keen to give the stair climber a try, start out by doing just a few minutes at a lower intensity. As your fitness improves, you can gradually begin boosting the intensity.
